a30d282237.q: Why did Austin Hensley move from Dayton to Beavercreek in 2015?
a30d282237.a: Austin moved to Beavercreek because he discovered that Dayton had a significant income tax deduction on his paycheck. He learned that only three cities in Ohio do not have an income tax, and Beavercreek, located six miles away, was one of them. When he changed his residency and moved to Beavercreek at the end of 2015, his paycheck increased by $60 every two weeks.

75abf31570.q: What is the sixth income tax attempt in Beavercreek and why does Austin Hensley oppose it?
75abf31570.a: The 2026 income tax proposal is the sixth attempt by Beavercreek to implement a municipal income tax, with previous attempts in 2020, 2022, and 2026. Austin opposes it because he believes that after two rejections at the ballot box, voters have expressed a democratic mandate, and the issue should die. He argues that all three recent attempts have had no substantive changes—always a property tax reduction in exchange for an income tax on workers, with the millage currently at 10 mils.

49842bcb9f.q: When was Beavercreek incorporated as a city and what charter provision did its founders establish regarding income tax?
49842bcb9f.a: Beavercreek was founded in 1980, and the founders wisely created a city charter provision that prevents any imposition of an income tax without explicit voter approval. Additionally, they placed municipal elections in odd-numbered years to lower turnout and increase participation from voters more tuned into local politics, making it easier for citizens to place ballot initiatives on the ballot.

b8ac1319b7.q: What alternative funding mechanism does Austin Hensley propose if property taxes are eliminated in Ohio?
b8ac1319b7.a: Austin proposes a sales tax at the county level that would be applied to non-essential purchases and apportioned to cities and townships based on population. However, he acknowledges he has not done the exact math and is not a state legislator. He notes that any such change would require action by the state legislature, as sales tax is only handled at the state level in Ohio.
